concept.body: The asymmetry to remember: to DISPROVE "all X are Y," one counterexample is enough. To PROVE it, examples never suffice — you need a reason covering every case. Confirming examples build confidence; they can't finish the job.

explanationVariants: One counterexample suffices to disprove a claim about every case.
"All X are Y" collapses the moment a single X fails to be Y.

widget.prompt: How many counterexamples does it take to disprove the claim "all swans are white"?

commonErrors.feedback: 1000 is far more than needed — a single non-white swan already breaks "all."
Zero found means the claim still stands. Disproving needs at least one exception: 1.

steps.body: You've seen a pattern hold ten times — is it always true? A **conjecture** is a pattern you suspect; a **proof** is a chain of reasoning that makes it certain. The gap between them is the whole game: no matter how many examples agree, one counterexample can still sink a conjecture. Examples build belief; only proof gives knowledge.

widget.prompt: Sort each statement: is it a CONJECTURE (pattern, not yet certain) or a PROOF (settled by reasoning)?

items.label: "I tried five triangles and the angles always summed to 180°"
items.feedback: Five confirming cases is evidence for a conjecture — it hasn't ruled out the sixth. That takes a proof.

items.label: "Since a straight angle is 180° and the three angles rearrange onto it, they must sum to 180°"
items.feedback: A reason covering EVERY triangle at once — that's a proof, not a tally of examples.

items.label: "Every prime I've checked so far is odd"
items.feedback: A pattern from examples — and a shaky one: 2 is a prime that's even. Conjectures can be wrong.

items.label: "n² is even whenever n is even, because n = 2k makes n² = 4k²"
items.feedback: An argument from the definition, true for all even n — a proof.

widget.missFeedback: Counting examples makes a conjecture; giving a reason that covers all cases makes a proof.

explanationVariants: A single counterexample disproves a universal conjecture — "all X are Y" fails the instant one X isn't Y.
One exception is fatal: it shows the claim isn't ALWAYS true, which is exactly what the conjecture asserted.

widget.prompt: A conjecture claims something is true for EVERY case. What is the smallest number of counterexamples needed to disprove it?

commonErrors.feedback: 100 would certainly do it, but it's overkill — a single case where the claim fails already breaks "every case."
Zero counterexamples means none was found — that doesn't DISPROVE it. You need at least one exception: 1.

widget.fallbackFeedback: One counterexample breaks a universal claim.

steps.body: Flip it around: how many examples PROVE a universal conjecture? **None ever can.** A million confirming cases still leave the million-and-first unchecked. Proof escapes the trap by reasoning about ALL cases at once — usually from definitions and established facts, not from a pile of instances.

widget.prompt: A student checks a conjecture on 1,000 cases and every one works. What has been established?

options.label: Strong evidence for the conjecture, but not a proof
options.feedback: 1,000 successes raise confidence, yet the 1,001st is still unchecked — universal truth needs reasoning, not tallying.

options.label: The conjecture is proven — 1,000 is plenty
options.feedback: A finite count never proves a claim about INFINITELY many cases — there's always a next case the examples didn't reach.

options.label: The conjecture is disproven
options.feedback: Every case WORKED, so nothing was disproven — but confirming cases don't prove it either. It stays a well-supported conjecture.

options.label: Nothing at all
options.feedback: 1,000 confirmations is real evidence — it just falls short of PROOF. It makes the conjecture very plausible.

steps.body: This is why constructions needed proofs, not just careful drawings. A drawing is one more confirming example; a proof — equal radii, congruent triangles, done — settles every case. The rest of this chapter builds the machinery: how to write a proof that a skeptic can't wriggle out of.

explanationVariants: A drawing is a single confirming example, subject to the same limit — it can't guarantee the construction works in EVERY case. Proof can.
No drawing, however careful, escapes the examples-don't-prove-universals trap; a logical argument does.

widget.prompt: Why couldn't a carefully measured construction be accepted on the drawing alone?

options.label: A drawing is just one more example, and examples can't prove a universal claim
options.feedback: The construction claims to work ALWAYS — one accurate drawing is a single case, so a general proof is required.

options.label: Drawings are never accurate enough to be useful
options.feedback: Drawings ARE accurate enough to suggest and check — they simply can't PROVE universality, which is a different limitation.

options.label: Measuring tools are illegal in geometry
options.feedback: Nothing forbids measuring — it's just that a measurement confirms one case, and proof needs all cases.

options.label: Proofs are shorter than drawings
options.feedback: Length isn't the issue — certainty is. A proof covers every case; a drawing covers one.

widget.prompt: "The angle bisector construction always works — I tested it on twenty different angles." This reasoning is…

options.label: evidence for the claim, but not a proof
options.feedback: Twenty successes support it, yet the twenty-first angle is still unchecked — universality needs a reason, not a tally.

options.label: a complete proof — twenty cases is thorough
options.feedback: A finite batch of test angles can't cover ALL angles — thoroughness in examples still isn't proof.

options.label: a disproof of the construction
options.feedback: Every test WORKED, so nothing was disproven — but confirming cases don't prove it either.

options.label: irrelevant to whether the construction works
options.feedback: Twenty confirmations are real evidence — they raise confidence, just short of proving universality.

hints: The conjecture: "every angle has a larger supplement than complement." Test angle sizes.
Supplement = 180 − a; complement = 90 − a. When is the supplement NOT larger?
Both differ by exactly 90 for any valid angle — so the supplement is ALWAYS 90 more. Is the claim actually true, or is the trap elsewhere?
explanationVariants: For any angle a (0 < a < 90), supplement = 180 − a and complement = 90 − a, differing by exactly 90 — the supplement is always larger, so the claim is actually TRUE and has no counterexample. The right answer is that no counterexample exists.
180 − a is always 90 more than 90 − a, for every valid a — the conjecture holds universally, so you cannot break it with any example.

widget.prompt: Conjecture: "For any acute angle, the supplement is exactly 90° larger than the complement." Which is the correct verdict?

options.label: It's true — for any angle a, (180 − a) − (90 − a) = 90, with no counterexample
options.feedback: The a's cancel: the difference is always 90, independent of the angle. No counterexample exists, and the algebra proves it.

options.label: False — a 45° angle is a counterexample
options.feedback: Check 45°: supplement 135, complement 45, difference 90 ✓. It confirms the claim, not breaks it.

options.label: False — a 30° angle is a counterexample
options.feedback: Check 30°: supplement 150, complement 60, difference 90 ✓. Another confirming case, not a counterexample.

options.label: It can't be decided without checking every angle
options.feedback: The algebra (180 − a) − (90 − a) = 90 covers EVERY angle at once — that's a proof, so no case-by-case check is needed.

takeaways: Conjecture = a pattern you suspect; proof = reasoning that makes it certain.
One counterexample disproves a universal; no finite pile of examples proves one.
A proof reasons about all cases at once — which is why constructions need them.
